one_line: A Rust validator that classifies payloads against twelve hand-written attack scenarios, regenerated by a fixture generator and run on every commit by CI.

sections.accomplishments: A green CI run and successful multi-file compilation on the first attempt, and completing the pipeline just as the month's AI token budget ran out.
sections.challenges: The whole framework was written and committed from a mobile device, so every pushed command had to work first time; runner compilation and dependency conflicts were the failure mode to avoid.
sections.how_we_built_it: 100% Rust. Engine logic in src/cvm.rs and src/main.rs; src/bin/gen_fixtures.rs generates clean and malicious fixtures; tests/simulation_matrix.rs runs the twelve scenarios; .github/workflows/test.yml provisions a runner, caches dependencies, compiles and executes the whole suite per change.
sections.inspiration: Complex systems behave predictably under stress, so a validator should be built around those stress patterns rather than around general input handling; the write-up reaches for a gambling-mechanics analogy for it.
sections.learned: Backend engineering, TDD and cloud automation are not desktop-bound; precise logic plus a mobile-and-AI workflow can carry the rest.
sections.what_it_does: Analyses binaries and payloads, classifies them against a fixed set of attack vectors, and reports a verdict per scenario; positioned as the drift-catching layer of a larger audit platform.
sections.what_next: Grow from twelve scenarios to a behavioural analysis suite, add live network anomaly tracking, status-code telemetry and real-time visualisation, and intercept threats in-flight.

testing: A real harness is described - a fixture generator plus a twelve-scenario matrix executed by CI on every commit - which is the right shape for this kind of validator. But the page links no repository, workflow or run id, so the green-checkmark claim cannot be checked, and a suite whose cases and fixtures are both authored by the system measures agreement with itself.
